seg_p0040_s0001: Jerome affirms that St. Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, τὸν τὴν οἰκουμένην σταδεύσαντα, καὶ τῷ περὶ πίστεως δρόμῳ τὸν κόσμον μικρὸν ἀποφήναντα [who traversed the inhabited world, and by his race for the faith made the world seem small] (as Basil of Seleucia speaks of him), "ran from ocean to ocean," "imitating his Lord and the sun of righteousness, of whom we read: His going forth is from the highest heaven, and his circuit reaches to the highest part of it, so that the earth would sooner fail than his zeal for preaching"; and that, after his first defense — which he himself mentions in the later epistle to Timothy — having been released by Nero, he preached the gospel of Christ in the regions of the West as well. The words of the apostle are: "At my first defense no one stood with me, but all forsook me. May it not be charged against them. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the preaching might be fulfilled, and all the Gentiles might hear." On which passage Theodoret says: "When," he says, "having made his appeal, he was sent from Festus to Rome, his defense was heard and he was acquitted, and he set out for Spain, and, running out to other peoples, brought them the light of doctrine"; and, as the same author adds elsewhere, "He brought benefit to the islands that lie in the sea." Whence Venantius Fortunatus says of him: He crossed the Ocean, even where the island makes a harbor, and the lands the Briton holds, and those of farthest Thule.
seg_p0040_s0002: And Sophronius, patriarch of Jerusalem, in his sermon on the feast of the apostles, indicates that Paul preached the gospel to the Spaniards and the Britons; this, however, I report on the credit of others, for I have not yet myself managed to see the source. The old translator of Chrysostom's sermon on Pentecost likewise hints that he ran from Spain "to the farthest parts" of the earth. Finally, "like some heavenly bird traversing the whole habitable world round about, his evangelical contest for Christ accomplished over thirty-five years," as Nicephorus writes, he at last completed his course by martyrdom at Rome under Nero.
seg_p0040_fn_001: Running through the furlongs of the habitable earth, and, by the course undertaken for the faith, displaying the narrow confines of the world. Basil of Seleucia, Oration 2 (or "On Adam, I").
seg_p0040_fn_004: Jerome, in his Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers, under "Paul"; and Hilduin, in his work on the Areopagite; and Ado, in his little book "On the Festivals of the Apostles."
